title: An Alternative To Time-Out
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In response to schools and districts banning traditional time-out as overly punitive, Linsin proposes 'observation mode' (OM), which he presents in two forms. The simplest is purely a rebranding — using the same time-out procedure taught in his elementary guide under a new, more accurately descriptive name, which he says satisfies most administrative pressure without changing anything substantive. The second form addresses situations where students cannot be physically moved from their seat, such as under Covid-related seating restrictions or unusually punitive-averse administrations: a seated version of OM in which the student remains in place but is excluded from discussions, group work, and games while still completing independent and listening work. He acknowledges this version is less effective than physically relocating a student, since the act of walking to another spot itself signals accepted responsibility, but argues it can still work because the real mechanism behind any consequence is consistent follow-through, not the specific consequence itself.
points: 'Observation mode' (OM) is proposed as a rebranded, administratively acceptable alternative to traditional time-out.
In its simplest form, OM is purely a name change applied to the same time-out procedure already taught in the elementary guide.
A seated version of OM excludes a student from discussions, group work, and games while keeping them in their seat, for situations where relocation isn't allowed.
Physically moving to a different location is considered more effective than a seated consequence because the act of moving itself signals accepted responsibility.
The real mechanism behind any consequence's effectiveness is consistent follow-through by the teacher, not the specific form the consequence takes.
quotes: I call it “observation mode” (OM). And it can be used in two different ways.
For the first time since we started SCM back in 2009, we’re hearing reports of administrators not wanting any accountability. This, of course, is a train wreck.

Meaning, they’re no longer allowed to participate in discussions, group work, learning games, etc. but are still responsible for all listening and independent work. Essentially, it’s time-out in their own seat.

It’s a way of conceding guilt and being prompted—by no longer being an active member of a class they like and enjoy being part of—to reflect on their misbehavior and resolve not to make the same mistake again.
You see, there is no magic in any consequence. The magic is in your follow through.
